identity.title: Timing and triggers (TiTrATE: episodic vs continuous, triggered vs spontaneous) rather than symptom quality; associated diplopia/dysarthria/dysphagia/hearing loss

technique.how: Instead of asking 'what kind of dizziness', ask: Is it there now continuously or does it come in discrete episodes? How long do episodes last (seconds, minutes, hours)? Is it brought on only by a trigger (head/position change, standing) or does it arise spontaneously? Then ask about diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, new hearing loss, headache or neck pain.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; screen for red-flag neurologic symptoms before deciding on examination pathway.

interpretation.positive_finding: Continuous acute vestibular syndrome demands HINTS-type eye examination for stroke; triggered brief episodes point to BPPV or orthostatic hypotension (test with Dix-Hallpike or orthostatic vitals); spontaneous episodes lasting minutes-hours suggest TIA, Meniere or arrhythmia. Any associated brainstem symptom raises stroke probability.
interpretation.negative_finding: A clear positional trigger with seconds-long episodes and no neurologic symptoms makes central causes unlikely, but isolated dizziness can still be a vertebrobasilar stroke.
interpretation.pitfalls: Symptom-quality descriptors (vertigo vs lightheadedness) are unreliable: 52% of ED patients changed their descriptor on retest after ~6 minutes, so do not triage on 'type'. Do not confuse 'worse with movement' (most vestibular causes) with 'only occurs with movement' (true trigger).
interpretation.changes_what: Determines which bedside exam follows: HINTS for continuous spontaneous, Dix-Hallpike for triggered episodic, orthostatic vitals for standing-triggered, ECG/monitoring for spontaneous episodic.

estimates.target_condition: 'Serious' cause of dizziness (stroke/TIA, arrhythmia, medication, seizure, other requiring admission) - composite predictor: older age OR lack of vertigo OR neurologic deficit
estimates.population: 125 ED patients with dizziness evaluated with a standardized 66-item history/exam/lab protocol
estimates.reference_standard: Emergency physician diagnosis modified by 1-month follow-up using predefined diagnostic criteria
estimates.quote: The best predictors, either older age, lack of vertigo, or neurologic deficit, could identify 86% of "serious" dizziness with 42% specificity.

sources.citation: Newman-Toker DE, Cannon LM, Stofferahn ME, Rothman RE, Hsieh YH, Zee DS. Imprecision in patient reports of dizziness symptom quality: a cross-sectional study conducted in an acute care setting. Mayo Clin Proc. 2007;82(11):1329-1340.
Newman-Toker DE, Edlow JA. TiTrATE: A Novel, Evidence-Based Approach to Diagnosing Acute Dizziness and Vertigo. Neurol Clin. 2015;33(3):577-599.
Herr RD, Zun L, Mathews JJ. A directed approach to the dizzy patient. Ann Emerg Med. 1989;18(6):664-672.
Kerber KA, Meurer WJ, Brown DL, et al. Stroke risk stratification in acute dizziness presentations: A prospective imaging-based study. Neurology. 2015;85(21):1869-1878.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a reassuring timing/trigger pattern alone to exclude stroke in patients with vascular risk factors, new headache/neck pain, or any brainstem symptom; obtain the targeted examination.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Acute continuous dizziness with any of diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb ataxia, new deafness or inability to walk unaided is a stroke pathway until proven otherwise; up to 20% of early DWI-MRI are false negative.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Duration and trigger reports were 'clear, consistent, and reliable' on retest whereas quality descriptors were not (Newman-Toker 2007); associated-symptom screening depends on directed questioning.

extraction_notes: TiTrATE (PMID 26231273) is a narrative/consensus framework with no accuracy numbers; entered as kind 'consensus'. The quantified support for preferring timing/triggers over quality is the reliability study (Newman-Toker 2007): 52% changed descriptor on retest, 62% selected >1 type; entered as an estimate with all accuracy fields null, hence partially_quantified. Herr 1989 composite (older age OR lack of vertigo OR neurologic deficit; sens 0.86, spec 0.42) is included because it is the only accessible ED accuracy figure involving associated neurologic deficit, but it mixes in a symptom-quality item ('lack of vertigo') that TiTrATE argues against - owner should weigh whether to keep it. No dedicated accuracy study of the episodic/continuous x triggered/spontaneous classification was found within budget. Tarnutzer 2011 CMAJ systematic review (PMID 21576300, PMC3114934) would supply history-feature accuracy for stroke in acute vestibular syndrome but the PMC deposit is abstract-only, so no numbers could be verified. Kerber 2015/2016 reports OR 2.54 (95% CI 1.06-6.08) for 'any other CNS features' - an odds ratio, not an LR, so cited but not entered as an estimate.
